passages.t: The fool, and how to answer him
passages.happening:
‘Like snow in summer and rain at harvest, honor does not befit a fool’ (verse 1). ‘Like a fluttering sparrow or darting swallow, an undeserved curse does not come to rest’ (verse 2).

Then two sayings side by side: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him” (verse 4), and “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes” (verse 5).

Sending a message by a fool is like cutting off your own feet (verse 6). ‘Like lame legs hanging limp is a proverb in the mouth of a fool’ (verse 7). Giving honor to a fool is like tying a stone into a sling (verse 8). ‘As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly’ (verse 11).

And the sharpest word comes last: ‘Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This chapter gathers three portraits the book has warned about since its first pages: the fool (verses 1-12), the slacker (13-16) and the deceiver (17-28). The fool, kesil, is not someone lacking intelligence but someone settled in folly who will not learn.

Snow in summer and rain at harvest are out of season and do harm. Honor given to a fool is just as out of place.

People in the ancient world feared curses, and many thought spoken words carried power in themselves. Verse 2 reassures the reader: a curse that is not deserved has nowhere to land, like a bird that flits about and never settles.

A message sent by a trusted servant was the only way to do business or diplomacy at a distance. A foolish messenger could garble it, offend the hearer or put the sender in danger.

Dogs were mostly scavengers, not pets, which gives verse 11 its force. And verse 12 turns the whole portrait on the reader. Worse than the fool is the person who is sure he is wise.
passages.later: Peter applies verse 11 to teachers who turned back after knowing the way: “A dog returns to its vomit” (2 Peter 2:22). And Paul warns against the man of verse 12: ‘If any of you thinks he is wise in this age, he should become a fool, so that he may become wise’ (1 Corinthians 3:18).
passages.hard:
Verses 4 and 5 give opposite advice. Is the Bible contradicting itself?

Verse 4 says not to answer a fool according to his folly, or you will become like him. Verse 5 says to answer a fool according to his folly, or he will become wise in his own eyes.

The collectors put these sayings next to each other on purpose, and ancient Jewish interpreters already discussed the tension. The Talmud records a debate over whether the book should be withdrawn because of it, and the answer given was that the two sayings apply to different situations.

That is the most common reading. Sometimes engaging a fool on his own terms drags you down to his level. Sometimes silence lets his folly stand unchallenged. Others suggest the two verses speak of different sides of an answer: refuse the fool's manner (verse 4), but expose his argument on its own terms (verse 5).

Either way, the pair teaches how to read the whole book. A proverb describes how life usually goes. It is not a rule for every case. Wisdom is the ability to judge which proverb fits the moment, and no single saying can supply that.
passages.asks: Verse 12 says the person most beyond help is the one wise in his own eyes. Ask where you are most sure you are right, and whether anyone is allowed to tell you otherwise. And ask, the next time someone foolish provokes you, which of verses 4 and 5 fits the moment.

passages.t: The slacker turns on his bed
passages.happening:
The slacker cries out that there is a lion in the road, a fierce lion loose in the public square (verse 13).

‘As a door turns on its hinges, so the slacker turns on his bed’ (verse 14). ‘The slacker buries his hand in the dish; it wearies him to bring it back to his mouth’ (verse 15). ‘The slacker is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer discreetly’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Four sayings in a row about the slacker, each with humorous exaggeration. He invents a lion in the street to avoid going out. He turns in bed like a door on its hinges, moving all the time and going nowhere. He is too tired to lift food to his mouth.

Lions did live in the region in biblical times, so the excuse was not impossible. It was simply convenient.

The last saying is the most serious. The slacker does not think he is lazy. He thinks he is wise, wiser than seven people who could set him straight. That links him to verse 12. His real trouble is not his bed but his certainty.
passages.later: Hebrews asks its readers not to become like him: ‘Then you will not be sluggish, but will imitate those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised’ (Hebrews 6:12).
passages.asks: The slacker always has a reason. Ask what lion you have invented to avoid something you know you should do. And ask whether you have dismissed good advice because you were sure you knew better.

passages.t: Meddlers, gossips, and smooth lips over a hateful heart
passages.happening:
‘Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own’ (verse 17). Like a madman shooting firebrands and deadly arrows is the man who deceives his neighbor and then says he was only joking (verses 18-19).

‘Without wood, a fire goes out; without gossip, a conflict ceases’ (verse 20). ‘Like charcoal for embers and wood for fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife’ (verse 21). ‘The words of a gossip are like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being’ (verse 22).

‘Like glaze covering an earthen vessel are burning lips and a wicked heart’ (verse 23). The hateful man hides behind gracious words, but ‘his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly’ (verse 26). ‘He who digs a pit will fall into it, and he who rolls a stone will have it roll back on him’ (verse 27). ‘A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth causes ruin’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
These verses move from the meddler and the prankster to the gossip, the quarreler and the flatterer. Each harms people with words.

Grabbing a passing dog by the ears was asking to be bitten. Stepping into someone else's fight is the same.

Pottery was the ordinary material of household vessels. A glaze, perhaps silver dross as some interpreters read the Hebrew, could make cheap clay look fine. Warm, smooth words over a wicked heart are the same kind of disguise.

Verse 22 repeats 18:8 word for word. And verse 20 is plain enough to remember: take away the fuel and the fire dies.
passages.later: The psalms describe the trap of verse 27: ‘He has dug a hole and hollowed it out; he has fallen into a pit of his own making’ (Psalm 7:15). And James says of the tongue what verses 20 and 21 picture: ‘Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze’ (James 3:5).
passages.asks: Without wood, a fire goes out. Ask what quarrel near you is being kept alive by words, and whether some of the wood is yours. And ask whether you have ever hurt someone and then called it a joke.
